applies_why: This text weighs the challenger's seed/loins chain against the defender's chain in a collision over a link (D6 vs C1, Acts 2:30), the exact chain-against-chain collision K-C governs.
quote: the challenger's seed/loins chain is footed but does not name Joseph as the begetter; the defender's chain is footed but rests on the woman-route inference
rule_words: the collision weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse; that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side
room: Phrases interpreted: 'weighs chain against chain by footing' together with 'the stating-verse test DG-61 retires... for either side' (and the definition's 'judged by its support, never by whether any verse, or the chain as a whole, states it word for word'). Reading one: 'does not name Joseph as the begetter' and 'rests on the woman-route inference' are footing-reach observations -- each chain's support simply does not reach its conclusion -- so the judge stayed on footing and is clean. Reading two: the judge first conceded each chain is footed, then made absence of explicit statement (no naming of Joseph; inference instead of statement) the operative ground of decision, which is the retired stating-verse test applied to both chains. I weighed the second reading because 'name' targets explicit statement and the 'is footed but' construction sets footing aside as the deciding ground.
why: The judge found both chains footed yet let each chain's failure to state its point in its own words ('does not name Joseph as the begetter'; 'rests on the woman-route inference' rather than stating it) decide the collision, which is the stating-verse test K-C retires at a judge's seat for either side, not a decision by footing.
